title: Electric current as a flow of charge practice

evidence_basis.originality_note: Original wire, electrolyte and ionised-gas contexts test the controlled definition and carrier model without copying official wording, values or diagrams and without requiring later charge formulas.

questions.prompt: State the SI base unit of electric current and give its unit symbol.
Which particles are the mobile charge carriers in a metal wire?
Which observation is sufficient to show that electric current exists through a chosen cross-section?

options.A: Uncharged particles move parallel to the cross-section
options.C: Charged particles remain stationary beside the section
options.D: The conductor contains fixed charged particles

questions.prompt: During equal time intervals, more charge passes section X than section Y. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The current at X is greater than the current at Y
options.B: The current at Y is greater than the current at X
options.D: The currents must be equal because the times are equal

questions.prompt: A metal wire carries an electric current.

figure.purpose: Assess identification of mobile and fixed charged particles in a metal.
figure.brief: Original black-and-white Cambridge-inspired line diagram. Show a magnified wire containing a regular array of large circles marked plus and several small solid dots. A dashed cross-section cuts across the wire. Include no unused labels, motion arrows or answers.
figure.alt_text: A magnified metal wire shows large positive lattice ions, small electron dots and a dashed cross-section.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Name the mobile charge carriers in the wire.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why the fixed positive ions do not provide a current through the dashed cross-section.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State what must happen at the dashed cross-section for the wire to have a non-zero current there.

questions.prompt: A beaker contains an electrolyte that conducts electricity.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Identify the charge carriers in the electrolyte and describe what they do when there is a current.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A student says, ‘Current is always a flow of electrons.’ Explain why this statement is not a complete description of current in the electrolyte.

questions.prompt: The diagram compares charge-carrier motion in three conducting materials and includes a second metal sample M2. The same short time interval is shown throughout.

figure.purpose: Assess the common carrier model across metal, electrolyte and ionised gas without later formulas.
figure.brief: Original black-and-white Cambridge-inspired line diagram. Show three boxed samples with a dashed cross-section in each. Sample M is a metal with electron dots crossing. Sample E is an electrolyte with positive and negative ion symbols crossing in opposite directions. Sample G is an ionised gas with ion and electron symbols crossing. Show sample M with visibly more charge-carrier crossings than a second small metal comparison M2. Do not label carrier names.
figure.alt_text: Three samples show different charged particles crossing dashed sections, plus two metals with different amounts of charge crossing in equal times.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: For samples M, E and G, identify the types of mobile charge carrier shown.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Use the definition of current to explain why all three samples can carry an electric current even though their carriers are different.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The same time interval is shown for M and M2. State which has the greater current, explain why, and give the SI unit symbol for current.
